lines.text: Ghana's gold weights hinted at proverbs.
Around 1800 in Kumasi, people paid in gold dust instead of coins.
lines.say: Around eighteen hundred in Koo mah see, people paid in gold dust instead of coins.

lines.text: Each side brought scales and weights to agree on a fair weight.
Smiths cast the weights in brass, using lost wax.
Some were shaped like chameleons or scorpions.
Smiths filed a little off or added lead to match the weight.
One design shows two crocodiles joined at a single stomach.
Its proverb says relatives fight over food that feeds them all.
Most weights are tiny, some only 3 centimeters long.
lines.say: Most weights are tiny, some only three centimeters long.

lines.text: Akan smiths used such weights from about 1400 to 1900.
lines.say: Akan smiths used such weights from about fourteen hundred to nineteen hundred.

post.caption: Ghana's gold weights hinted at proverbs. Around 1800 in Kumasi, people paid in gold dust instead of coins. Each side brought scales and weights to agree on a fair weight. Smiths cast the weights in brass, using lost wax. Some were shaped like chameleons or scorpions. Smiths filed a little off or added lead to match the weight. One design shows two crocodiles joined at a single stomach. Its proverb says relatives fight over food that feeds them all. Most weights are tiny, some only 3 centimeters long. Akan smiths used such weights from about 1400 to 1900. Photo: Brooklyn Museum, CC BY 3.0.
